mohair.origin: Mohair is the hair of the Angora breed of the domestic goat, Capra hircus, whose name is tied to the Ankara region of Anatolia. Angora-type goats are kept elsewhere too, including the Markhoz, an indigenous Iranian breed whose mohair is used in ceremonial garments. Angora goats reached the United States from Turkey in 1849, and South Africa built a large industry, although researchers there describe its Angora as the most efficient fiber producer but least hardy small-stock breed in southern Africa. Mohair should not be confused with angora, which is rabbit hair.
mohair.structure: Mohair is a keratin fiber in a fleece that also contains medullated fibers. Studies of Angora fleeces distinguish continuous and interrupted medullated fibers and kemp, a coarse, heavily medullated fiber, and they find that diameter, medullation, brightness and yield all vary over the body, with the midrib giving a representative sample. Compared with fine wool, mohair has little crimp and flatter, less prominent cuticle scales, which give luster and a weaker felting tendency. Diameter coarsens as the goat ages, which is why kid, young goat and adult mohair are sold separately; an Italian trial measured secondary fibers of about 16.5 to 18 microns in kids around five months old.
mohair.process: Angora goats are commonly shorn about every six months; in an Argentine study the first two shearings were at 12 and 18 months of age. Fleeces are skirted and classed by age, fineness, length and freedom from kemp and vegetable matter, then scoured, carded and usually combed for worsted spinning, where length and luster suit smooth suiting yarns and brushed loop yarns. Research tools have been built to speed classing: near-infrared spectroscopy predicted clean mohair yield and diameter from fleece samples, and a modified optical fiber diameter analyser estimated medullation from fiber opacity. Chemical defleecing with mimosine has also been studied experimentally as an alternative to shearing.
mohair.performance: Mohair shares wool's hygroscopic keratin chemistry, acid dye affinity and self-extinguishing flame behavior, but its smooth surface and straight fibers give luster, resilience and resistance to crushing, which suits pile fabrics and upholstery. Low crimp and smoother scales make it felt less readily than wool, although it can still felt under heat, moisture and agitation. Medullated and kemp fibers are highly undesirable in mohair because they are stiff, feel prickly and appear as chalky white fibers that take dye differently. Like other animal fibers it is attacked by clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae.
mohair.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) behave like wool. Under light or scanning electron microscopy mohair shows thin, flat scales with few visible scale edges, and projection microscopy counts medullated and kemp fibers; opacity-based instruments do this faster but need separate calibrations for mohair and wool. Peptide profiling by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry has distinguished mohair from cashmere, wool, yak, camel, angora and alpaca, including dyed samples and 50% blends. Confusion with angora rabbit hair is a naming error, not a fiber similarity.
mohair.labeling: The US Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 includes hair of the Angora goat in its definition of wool, and the specialty name mohair may be used in place of wool with its percentage. In the EU, Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists mohair as a named fine animal hair, while the name angora refers to rabbit hair, so the two cannot be substituted. Textile Exchange's Responsible Mohair Standard is a voluntary certification covering goat welfare and land management with chain of custody; certificate scope should be checked for each product.
mohair.past: Mohair's breed and name trace to Anatolia, and trade and breeding later moved much production elsewhere. In the United States, Angora goats arrived from Turkey in 1849, and research and performance testing were based at Texas agricultural stations. A federal incentive program kept producer returns relatively constant at an average of about 10 US dollars per kilogram, and a 1996 review questioned profitability once final payments ended that year. In South Africa, research on winter stock losses linked the Angora's poor tolerance of prolonged cold to two CYP17 enzyme isoforms that impair cortisol production, a physiological explanation for the breed's fragility.
